paras: The Greenville lynching of July 1895 was a killing in Greenville, apparently in South Carolina, that took place on a Monday morning shortly before July 23, 1895, and that a church paper's correspondent called "the recent lynching in Greenville." The surviving coverage names no victim, accusation or perpetrators. It is known only from a pastor's sermon and a Methodist paper's editorial and letters, which condemned lynching.

In a sermon on "infidelity" reported by the Greenville Daily News on July 23, a Greenville pastor said that visitors "from darkest Africa or cruel Turkey" who had stood on the town's streets "last Monday morning" would not have taken it for a Christian land. He called what happened "this outrage and horrible murder" and "the unlawful taking of human life," but did not name the victim or say who had done it. By his account, "scores and hundreds" of people condemned the outrage while as many tried to justify it.

No report of an inquest, arrest or trial appears in the coverage. The Southern Christian Advocate of Charleston ran an editorial condemning the lynching, which drew letters of agreement from correspondents named Berry and J. M. Steadman.

Only church papers in South Carolina carried the episode in the coverage found, and they treated it as an occasion for moral argument rather than news. The Baptist Courier of Columbia reprinted the pastor's sermon on August 1 under the heading "Murder and Lynching," with subheads on "The Cowardice of Christiana [Christians]" and "Duties Shirked." The sermon blamed the killing on "infidelity," on lawyers and juries that freed murderers, and on newspapers that said "mob law and lynching under certain circumstances is justifiable."

In the Southern Christian Advocate of August 22, Steadman's letter, dated August 3 and titled "Another View of Lynching," agreed that the editorial's censure "was just and was not too severe." He called lynching "as now practiced" both "cruel and unjust" and urged lynchers to "stop lynching poor negroes who will be punished." The remark was general; neither text states the Greenville victim's race. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

Only A2 explicitly calls the Greenville episode a lynching; A1 is an independent local source but its link to the same episode is inferred from place, timing and its 'Murder and Lynching' heading.

accounts.label: Greenville pastor's sermon
accounts.gist: A Greenville pastor said that 'last Monday morning' the town had seen an 'outrage and horrible murder' that he called the fruit of 'infidelity', and condemned those who justified mob law and lynching.

accounts.label: Methodist correspondent
accounts.gist: J. M. Steadman endorsed the Advocate's editorial condemning 'the recent lynching in Greenville' and argued that lynching as practiced was 'both cruel and unjust'.

framing.detail: Printed under the heading 'Murder and Lynching' with the subheads 'The Cowardice of Christiana [Christians]' and 'Duties Shirked', the sermon called the episode an 'outrage and horrible murder'.
The Advocate's correspondent called the editorial's censure 'just', called lynching 'cruel and unjust' and 'our disgrace', and urged an end to 'lynching poor negroes who will be punished'.
